attempts.user_message:
Please review the following manuscript. I've poured months of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b09/review-experiment-jazl1sgc/call-f0a256ff3d5740d2b4b070da82755558/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'ls -la . manuscript.pdf .agents && command -v pdftotext && command -v pdftoppm && command -v python3'

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import sys, importlib.util, shutil
print(sys.executable)
for name in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL']:
 print(name, importlib.util.find_spec(name))
for name in ['pdftoppm','pdftotext','pdfinfo','gs']:
 print(name, shutil.which(name))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES', len(reader.pages))
print('METADATA', reader.metadata)
chunks=[]
for i,page in enumerate(reader.pages,1):
 text=page.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02}.txt').write_text(text)
 chunks.append(f'\\n\\n======= PAGE {i} =======\\n{text}')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(chunks))
print(''.join(chunks[:3]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from fractions import Fraction
p=Fraction(1,2)
singleton_f1_average=p
population_f1=2*p/(1+p)
print('Perfect calibration, all predictions positive, class prevalence 1/2:')
print('Equation (1) using per-observation F1:', singleton_f1_average)
print('Population F1:', population_f1)
print('Conditional absolute label residual:', p*abs(1-p)+(1-p)*abs(p))
print('Absolute conditional calibration residual:', abs(p-p))
PY
"

strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment problem: estimating classifier performance when production labels are unavailable. Combining density-ratio estimation with weighted calibration is a sensible approach under covariate shift and adequate support overlap.

The evaluation includes 959 model–dataset combinations and 36,557 production chunks. PAPE achieves the best reported results across all six Table 1 criteria; compared with IW, RMSSTE decreases from 1.42 to 1.31 for accuracy, 1.56 to 1.45 for AUROC, and 1.70 to 1.35 for F1.

IW uses the same density-ratio estimator, while CBPE removes weighting, providing useful comparisons that help isolate the proposed combination's benefit. Analyses by shift magnitude and sample size add practical insight.

The manuscript describes temporal splits and filtering, links a code repository, and explicitly acknowledges concept shift, support mismatch, and estimation uncertainty. These limitations are useful disclosures. The reported public-data experiments raise no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central formula does not support the claimed applicability to arbitrary metrics. Equations (1)–(2) cover expectations of per-observation quantities, whereas F1 is a nonlinear ratio and AUROC requires pairwise comparisons. For example, with all-positive predictions and perfectly calibrated probability 0.5, averaging singleton F1 values gives 0.5, while population F1 is 2/3. Explicit estimators and appropriate justification for F1 and AUROC are missing, leaving two of the three evaluated metrics disconnected from the stated algorithm.

The theoretical guarantee concerns an assumed target-calibrated function, without controlling the density-ratio and calibration errors introduced by the implemented procedure. Equation (4) also incorrectly equates expected absolute label residual with absolute conditional calibration bias; these differ even under perfect calibration. The underlying additive-metric argument is repairable, but the current presentation overstates what has been established.

Important implementation choices are absent from the manuscript: the density-ratio classifier, calibrator family and loss, hyperparameters, preprocessing, and weight stabilization. Algorithm 1 obtains density-ratio predictions on the classifier's training inputs without specifying safeguards against overfitting. Although a repository is linked, the description alone does not establish a reproducible implementation or explain sensitivity to these central choices.

The experiments provide substantial scale within one data family but limited evidence of generality. Temporal changes in census data need not preserve p(y|x), and no controlled experiment with known covariate shift isolates the proposed mechanism. Sample-size robustness is examined for only one selected case. These results do not adequately support broad claims across data types and classification settings.

Statistical reporting is insufficient to assess the reliability and distribution of the gains. Table 1 pools errors across chunks, thereby giving larger datasets more influence, and provides no uncertainty intervals or dataset-level distribution of improvements. The unit of analysis for the Wilcoxon test is unspecified despite shared observations across model variants and repeated chunks within cases; reporting p = 0.0 does not resolve these dependencies.

Originality and scope need sharper positioning. Density-ratio estimation is standard, and the weighted-calibration transfer property is attributed to prior work [11], but the additional insight beyond their combination is not clearly established. The abstract also claims reliance only on predictions and probability estimates, although Algorithm 1 requires input features, and claims no assumptions about the shift despite requiring covariate shift and support overlap. Together with the metric-definition and reproducibility gaps, these issues outweigh the promising empirical results.
